comments.author: @johncostello2948
comments.text: As a retired patent attorney, I would say that the actual monetary success of an invention is greatly dependent on the person or people behind the invention.  If that person happens to be a solo inventor with little business acumen, and little understanding of a particular market, often those situations are a 3-5% possibility of a monetary return. If the invention is from a company with a solid team who knows their market, then they can often consistently have many more winners than losers. Also, for the solo inventors, if they have worked in an industry and know its needs from experience, and invent to fill those needs, then those were the most successful solo inventors in my experience. It is really a matter of who is the jockey, not the horse, that determines success. Ultimately, the patent is only an insurance policy, should an invention reach success, and need to defend against copyists. Nothing nefarious in that, so implying that patent attorneys are "shysters" etc., is not especially fair.

comments.text: I will tell you another thing patent attorneys don’t want you to know. They don’t want your work…if you are a solo inventor. Good patent attorneys want to work with a client that has repeat business and not just a one off invention. Solo inventors take too much time and end up being much less profitable compared to medium to large companies. Many good attorneys won’t even take on small clients for just this reason. And solo inventors are notorious for not paying their bills. Patents are expensive!

comments.author: @madflysports8458
comments.text: Let me tell you what they actually don’t want you to know. Most of the time they think your invention has little to no chance of being a success and the patent is a waste of money, but they will still do a good job no matter what. Because the success of your product is determined by so much more than the patent. Success is determined by the marketing, the cost to produce, consumer demand, etc and the patent has very little to do with that. Patents are gambling with slightly better odds.

comments.author: @madflysports8458
comments.text: Great video and interesting take from an inventor’s perspective. Sadly, no matter what you ask you will almost never know if you have a good patent attorney. You have to have a solid understanding of patents and what it takes to get one before you can tell a good patent attorney from a bad one. And a previous client’s success says little to nothing about the quality of the patent itself. Frankly, inventors are at a huge disadvantage knowing who to hire. If you hire a big GP firm you will drastically overpay. I would suggest finding an IP boutique firm that specializes in patents as you have a better chance of getting a decent patent attorney there. This topic could literally take hours to discuss.

comments.author: @toddtkelly
comments.text: This is not really accurate or fair. What you are saying is analogous to a book author having a conflict of interest with the book editor. The author wants to publish, get the story out, and monetize the book. The editor, wants to provide quality assurance for the author. That is what a good patent attorney is doing. There is NO money in a badly drafted patent. Second,  asking the patent drafter how often they have "Protected the success" is a bullshit question.  A well drafted patent, will prevent other patents from being approved. Patents carve out a property line, other people working in the  field have to work around that property line, and there is no way to know when do that unless they can earn a patent on a new invention. If that invention crosses the property line, it may lead to litigation or even a license deal. . .. if it goes to litigation, that is a sub-specialty, and most patent drafters only assist the litigators at best.
